summary.text: Cryptography is the practice and study of techniques for secure communication when adversaries are present.
Classic cryptography turns readable plaintext into unintelligible ciphertext, which can be read only by reversing the process with the right key.
Modern designs rest on mathematical problems that are hard to break in practice, which makes them computationally secure.

facts.label: Cast of characters
facts.value: Alice sends, Bob receives, Eve eavesdrops

facts.label: Everyday uses
facts.value: Electronic commerce, payment cards, digital currencies, passwords

facts.label: Unbreakable but awkward
facts.value: The one-time pad cannot be broken, yet is hard to use

items.prompt: Two friends use a scrambling method that never changes and has no secret setting. Their rival learns which method they use. What follows?

options.label: The rival still needs a lucky guess
The method is stronger the more widely it is known
The messages can trivially be broken
Only the sender's messages are at risk

items.explain: Ciphers without variable keys can be trivially broken with only knowledge of the cipher used, so keys matter in practice as well as in theory.

items.prompt: A spy receives a page of nonsense letters and runs the process backward to read the message. What are the terms for the page and the process?

options.label: The page is plaintext and the process is encryption
The page is a key and the process is a cipher
The page is ciphertext and the process is encryption
The page is ciphertext and the process is decryption

items.explain: Encryption turns plaintext into unintelligible ciphertext, and decryption is the reverse, moving back from ciphertext to plaintext.

items.prompt: A scheme could in theory be cracked, but doing so would be infeasible in actual practice. How is such a scheme described?

options.label: Information-theoretically secure
Computationally secure
Insecure
Non-repudiated

items.explain: A well-designed scheme that is breakable in theory but not in practice is termed computationally secure.

items.prompt: A scheme exists that cannot be broken even with unlimited computing power. Why doesn't everyone simply use it?

options.label: It is far harder to use in practice than good computationally secure schemes
It is known to break once computers get quick enough
It only protects messages that are written in a single language
It has been made illegal in every country on earth, so nobody may

items.explain: Information-theoretically secure schemes such as the one-time pad are much more difficult to use in practice than the best theoretically breakable but computationally secure ones.

items.prompt: A designer says a cryptographic scheme, once built, can be left alone for good. What is the problem with that view?

options.label: Schemes only keep working if they are rebuilt every single day
Faster computers and better factoring methods force re-examination
Keys expire after sending a fixed number of messages in total
Governments reset and replace all schemes each year as routine

items.explain: Theoretical advances, such as improvements in integer factorization algorithms, and faster computing require designs to be continually reevaluated and adapted if necessary.

items.prompt: Why have many governments classified cryptography as a weapon and limited its use or export?

options.label: Because it can only be run on military computers
Because it is too slow for civilians to use
Because it can serve as a tool for espionage and sedition
Because it cannot be used for commerce

items.explain: Its potential use as a tool for espionage and sedition led many governments to treat it as a weapon and limit or prohibit its use and export.
